items.prompt: What is the probability of an event that cannot possibly happen?
rubric: An impossible event has probability 0.
Distractor 1 confuses impossible with certain; 0.5 is an even chance.

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
rubric: One favourable outcome out of six equally likely outcomes gives 1/6.
1/4 and 4/6 mistakenly use the face value as the count.

items.prompt: For independent events A and B, which formula gives P(A and B)?

options.label: P(A) - P(B)
P(A) / P(B)
P(A) x P(B)
P(A) + P(B)

rubric: Independent events multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).
Addition is the rule for mutually exclusive events with 'or'.

items.prompt: In how many different orders can 3 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?
rubric: 3 and 9 come from adding or squaring instead of using a factorial.

items.prompt: What is the expected value of a random variable?

options.label: Its largest value minus its smallest
Its middle value in sorted order
Its probability-weighted average value
The outcome with the highest probability

rubric: Expected value is the sum of each value times its probability.
The highest-probability outcome is the mode, the middle value is the median, and the largest minus smallest is the range; each is a different summary of a distribution.

items.prompt: Which of these numbers could be a valid probability of an event? Select all that apply.
rubric: Probabilities must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive.
1.3 exceeds 1 and -0.2 is negative, so neither is valid.

items.prompt: A bag holds 3 red marbles and 5 blue marbles, all the same size. Without looking, Maya draws one marble at random. What is the probability that the marble is red?
rubric: Favourable outcomes 3 divided by total 8 gives 3/8.
3/5 compares red to blue (odds) instead of to the total.

items.prompt: Why must the probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1?

options.label: Because all outcomes are equally likely, so each gets an equal share
Because probabilities get rescaled after the fact to total 1
Because one outcome must occur, and outcomes can't overlap
Because each outcome needs a probability of at least one half

rubric: The sample space covers all possibilities, so some outcome happens with certainty.
Outcomes need not be equally likely; the sum rule still holds.

items.prompt: You count the number of heads in 10 flips of a fair coin. Which distribution models this count?

options.label: Poisson
Uniform
Binomial
Geometric

rubric: A fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes and constant p is binomial.
Geometric counts trials until the first success, not successes in a fixed number.

items.prompt: What does P(A | B) = 0.3 mean?

options.label: A occurs 30% of the time when B has occurred
Either A or B occurs 30% of the time overall
A and B both occur 30% of the time overall
B occurs 30% of the time when A has occurred

rubric: P(A | B) is the probability of A given that B has occurred.
Distractors confuse it with joint probability or reverse the condition.

items.prompt: A fair coin lands heads three times in a row. What is the probability the next flip is heads?

options.label: 1/2, because each flip is independent of earlier flips
More than 1/2, because the coin seems to be on a streak
Less than 1/2, because tails is now due to balance out
1/16, because four heads in a row is very unlikely

rubric: Flips are independent, so past results do not change the next flip.
The gambler's fallacy and hot-hand beliefs drive the other options.

items.prompt: In which situation does the order of selection matter, so a permutation is the right counting tool?

options.label: Choosing 2 people from a group to form a committee
Choosing 4 pizza toppings from a menu of 10 options
Choosing a president and a vice president
Choosing 3 lottery numbers drawn as an unordered set

rubric: Different roles make A-then-B different from B-then-A, so order matters.
The other options select an unordered group, which calls for combinations.

items.prompt: Events A and B are independent. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.

options.label: P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B)
P(A | B) = P(A)
A and B can never occur together
Knowing B happened does not change the probability of A

rubric: Independence means B gives no information about A, so P(A | B) = P(A).
Never occurring together is mutually exclusive, a different idea.

items.prompt: A carnival game costs nothing to enter. It pays $10 with probability 0.1 and $0 otherwise, so its expected value is $1. Sam plays it many hundreds of times. What does the expected value of $1 tell Sam?

options.label: He will win $1 on about 10% of plays
His average winnings per play should settle near $1
He will win at least $1 in every group of ten plays
His total winnings will be exactly $1 per play after a few hundred plays

rubric: Expected value is the long-run average outcome per play.
Other options treat it as a guaranteed or per-play result.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes two independent events A and B?

options.label: P(A and B) = 0, because the two events can never both happen together
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), because the events share no outcomes at all
P(A) = P(B), because both events are equally likely to occur overall
P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B), so one event does not change the other's chance

rubric: Independence means the joint probability is the product of the individual probabilities.
Distractors confuse independence with mutual exclusivity or equal probability.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say that two events are mutually exclusive?

options.label: Learning that one occurred makes the other more likely to occur
The two events cannot both occur on the same single trial
Learning that one occurred does not change the other's probability
Together the two events cover every possible outcome of the trial

rubric: Mutually exclusive events share no outcomes, so they cannot both happen.
Distractors describe positive dependence, independence, or exhaustive events.

items.prompt: What does P(A | B) represent?

options.label: The probability of A, given that B is known to have occurred
The probability that both A and B occur on the same trial
The probability of B occurring after A has already occurred
The probability that A occurs whether or not B occurs

rubric: P(A | B) is the probability of A restricted to cases where B happened.
Distractors confuse it with the joint probability, the reversed condition, or the unconditional probability.

items.prompt: What does the expected value of a random variable tell you?

options.label: The exact value you are guaranteed to see on the next trial
The long-run average value over many repetitions of the process
The single outcome that is most likely on any one trial
The middle value when all possible outcomes are sorted in order

rubric: Expected value is the long-run average, weighted by probability.
Distractors describe the mode, the median, or a guaranteed outcome.

items.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 10 times. The variable X is the number of heads. Which distribution fits X best?

options.label: Normal, because the number of heads is a continuous measurement that can take any value
Uniform, because every coin flip is equally likely to land heads or tails each time
Binomial, because there are a fixed number of independent two-outcome trials
Geometric, because we count the flips needed until the first head finally appears

rubric: Fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes and constant probability gives a binomial.
Distractors misuse uniform, geometric (waiting time) or normal (continuous).

items.prompt: Which statements about basic probability rules are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: A very unlikely event can have a negative probability value
The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1
For any event A, P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
A certain event has a probability greater than 1 in total

rubric: Total probability is 1 and the complement rule holds.
Probabilities are never negative or above 1; the distractors break these bounds.

items.prompt: A medical test has a sensitivity of 0.95. A clinic manager reads this figure in a report and wants to know what it means for the people who are tested at the clinic.

options.label: Of people who are healthy, 95% test negative on the test
Of all people tested, 95% receive a correct result either way
Of people who truly have the disease, 95% test positive
Of people who test positive, 95% truly have the disease

rubric: Sensitivity is P(positive | disease).
Distractors reverse the condition (predictive value), or describe overall accuracy or specificity.

items.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
rubric: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes sum to 7, giving 1/6.
Distractors undercount the pairs or use 7 as the numerator.

items.prompt: A club of 5 people must choose a committee of 3, where order does not matter. How many different committees are possible?
rubric: Use combinations: C(5,3) = 10.
60 is the ordered count (permutations); other values come from miscalculation.

items.prompt: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A or B)?
rubric: Distractors forget to subtract the overlap or report only the joint probability.

items.prompt: A game pays $6 if a fair die shows a 6, and otherwise you lose $1. What is the expected net result per play?

options.label: Gain of $0.17
Loss of $0.17
Gain of $1.00
Loss of $5.00

rubric: Distractors make sign errors or ignore the probability weights.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.40. What is P(A | B)?
rubric: Distractors multiply instead of dividing or return the joint probability.

items.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn one after the other. Which calculations of P(both red) are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Without replacement: (3/5)(3/5) = 9/25
With replacement: (3/5)(2/4) = 3/10
With replacement: (3/5)(3/5) = 9/25
Without replacement: (3/5)(2/4) = 3/10

rubric: Without replacement the second draw has 2 red of 4; with replacement it stays 3 of 5.
Distractors swap the two cases.

items.prompt: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws, and each shot is independent. She takes 3 free throws in a drill. The coach wants the probability that she makes exactly 2 of them.
rubric: Distractors omit the factor of 3 arrangements or compute a different count.

items.prompt: Two cards are dealt without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are hearts?
rubric: 1/16 comes from wrongly treating the draws as with replacement.

items.prompt: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 5 women and 3 men. What is the probability that it contains at least one man?
rubric: 5/28 and similar values come from counting only part of the cases or mixing up the complement.

items.prompt: Each of 4 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.3. What is the probability of exactly 1 success?
rubric: 0.1029 omits the factor 4 for the position of the success.

items.prompt: 2% of a population has a condition. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 10% of people who do not. A person tests positive. What is the probability they have the condition?

options.label: 2%, the base rate
90%, the sensitivity
1.8%, the true positives
About 15.5%

rubric: 90% confuses P(positive | condition) with P(condition | positive), ignoring the low base rate.

items.prompt: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2, pays $2 with probability 0.5, and otherwise costs the player $5. What is the expected net payoff per play?
rubric: $3.00 ignores the loss term; -$1.50 includes only the loss.

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled twice. Which events have probability exactly 1/6? Select all that apply.

options.label: The first roll is a 6
The sum of the rolls is 6
The sum of the rolls is 7
At least one roll is a 6
The two rolls show the same number

rubric: Equal rolls: 6/36, sum 7: 6/36, first roll 6: 6/36, all equal 1/6.
Sum 6 has 5/36 and at least one 6 has 11/36.

items.prompt: A batch holds 10 parts, 3 of them defective. An inspector pulls 2 parts at random without putting any back. She wants the probability that exactly one of the two is defective.
rubric: 21/50 (0.42) results from treating the draws as with replacement.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A or B) = 0.7. Which conclusion is justified?

options.label: Dependent, since P(A or B) = 0.7 is not equal to 0.5 + 0.4
Mutually exclusive, since the union 0.7 is less than 1
Independent, since P(A and B) = 0.2 equals P(A)P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4
Independent, since P(A or B) = 0.7 is larger than both P(A) and P(B)

rubric: Inclusion-exclusion gives P(A and B) = 0.2, which equals the product, so A and B are independent.
The distractors confuse independence with exclusivity or use the union alone.

items.prompt: A student says P(at least one 6 in four fair die rolls) = 4 × 1/6 = 2/3. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.label: The sum is right but should be divided by 4, giving 1/6
The correct value is 4 × (1/6) × (5/6)^3, about 0.39, since the six must appear once
Adding ignores overlap among the events; the correct value is 1 - (5/6)^4, about 0.52
The rolls should be multiplied, giving (1/6)^4, about 0.0008

rubric: The four events are not mutually exclusive, so use the complement: 1 - (5/6)^4.
The exactly-one answer ignores outcomes with two or more sixes.

items.prompt: A family has two children, with equally likely, independent sexes. Given that at least one is a girl, P(both girls) is 1/3, not 1/2. Why?

options.label: The first child's sex shifts the second's chance of a girl, lowering it from 1/2
The condition reduces the outcomes to GG, GB, BG, equally likely, and only one is two girls
Boys are slightly more common, which lowers the chance of two girls to one in three
Independence fails once a condition is given, so the second child's sex follows from the first

rubric: Conditioning leaves GG, GB, BG equally likely, so P(GG) = 1/3.
The distractors invent dependence between births or bias in sex.

items.prompt: The number of aces in a 5-card hand dealt from a standard 52-card deck needs a probability model. Which model fits, and why?

options.label: Geometric, since we count the cards dealt until the first ace appears
Binomial with n = 5 and p = 1/13, since each card dealt is an ace with the same chance 4/52
Poisson, since aces are rare events occurring within a fixed hand of cards
Hypergeometric, since cards are drawn without replacement so draws are dependent

rubric: Sampling without replacement from a finite population is hypergeometric.
Binomial wrongly assumes independent draws.

items.prompt: Var(X) = 4 and Y = 2X. A colleague computes Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) = 20. What is Var(X+Y)?

options.label: 36, since X+Y = 3X, so Var(X+Y) = 9 × 4
20, since Var(X) + Var(Y) = 4 + 16, and variances always add for sums
12, since X+Y = 3X and variance scales linearly: Var(3X) = 3 × 4
16, since Y = 2X is the larger term, so Var(Y) = 16 sets the total

rubric: Variances add only for independent variables; here X+Y = 3X, so Var = 9·4 = 36.
12 forgets that variance scales with the square of the constant.

items.prompt: Which statements about events A and B, each with positive probability, are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: If A and B are independent, P(A|B) = P(A)
If A and B are independent, they cannot be mutually exclusive
P(A|B) = P(B|A) always holds
If A and B are mutually exclusive, they are independent
If P(A) = P(B), then P(A|B) = P(B|A)

rubric: Independent events with positive probabilities have P(A and B) > 0, so they are not exclusive; independence gives P(A|B) = P(A); equal marginals make both conditionals equal P(A and B)/P(A).
Exclusive events have P(A|B) = 0 ≠ P(A), so they are dependent.

items.prompt: Machine M1 makes 60% of a plant's parts with a 2% defect rate; M2 makes 40% with a 5% defect rate. An inspector finds a defective part and assumes it came from M1 because M1 makes most of the output. Which is the best analysis?

options.label: M1 is more likely, about 75%, because its 60% output share outweighs the small gap in defect rates
The sources are equally likely, 50%, because a defect can occur on either machine at random
M2 is more likely, about 62.5%, since its higher defect rate outweighs its smaller output
M1 is more likely, about 60%, because the chance a defect came from M1 equals its output share

rubric: P(M2|D) = 0.02/(0.012+0.02) = 0.625, so M2 is the likelier source.
The M1 options ignore that the defect rate weights each machine's contribution.

items.prompt: A family has two children. Assume sex and birth weekday are independent and uniform. You learn that at least one child is a girl born on a Tuesday. What is the probability that both children are girls?
rubric: P(both girls and at least one Tuesday girl) = 13/196 and P(at least one Tuesday girl) = 27/196, so the answer is 13/27.
1/2 and 1/3 ignore how the extra weekday detail changes the counting of equally likely cases.

items.prompt: A student computes P(at least one six in 4 rolls of a fair die) as 4 x 1/6 = 2/3. Which diagnosis of the error is correct?

options.label: The events 'six on roll i' overlap, so adding their probabilities counts multi-six outcomes more than once
The probabilities should be multiplied, because 'at least one' requires every roll to be a six in turn
The rolls depend on each other, so each roll's probability must be conditioned on the earlier rolls before adding
The sum should be divided by 4, because averaging over the four rolls gives the chance that any one roll is a six

rubric: The events are not mutually exclusive, so simple addition overcounts; the correct value is 1 - (5/6)^4.
Distractors target false dependence between rolls and confusing 'at least one' with 'all'.

items.prompt: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A or B) = 0.7. What is P(A given B)?
rubric: 0.2 is the joint probability and 0.4 is P(B|A), which come from stopping early or swapping the conditioning.

items.prompt: You count hearts among 5 cards from a standard deck, once drawing with replacement and once without. Which comparison of the two counts is correct?

options.label: Same mean of 1.25 and same variance, because each single draw has probability 1/4 of being a heart in both cases
Same mean of 1.25, and the variance is smaller without replacement because the draws are negatively dependent
The mean is lower without replacement because hearts removed lower the chance, but the variance is identical
Same mean of 1.25, and the variance is larger without replacement because removing cards makes outcomes more spread

rubric: Linearity gives the same mean, but without replacement the indicators are negatively correlated, so variance shrinks by (52-5)/(52-1).
Distractors assume that equal single-draw marginals imply equal variance, or that dependence raises spread.

items.prompt: 1% of units on a line are faulty. A scanner flags 90% of faulty units and also flags 9% of good units. A unit is flagged. About what is the probability that it is faulty?

options.label: about 91%
about 50%
about 9%
about 1%

rubric: P(faulty|flag) = 0.009/(0.009 + 0.0891), about 9%, because false flags from the large good group dominate.
90% confuses sensitivity with the posterior; 91% subtracts the false-positive rate from 1.

items.prompt: X is uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: X and Y are dependent because P(Y=0 | X=0) = 1 but P(Y=0) = 1/3
X and Y are independent because their covariance is zero
Cov(X, Y) = 0
E[XY] differs from E[X]E[Y]
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)

rubric: Cov = E[X^3] - E[X]E[X^2] = 0, so variances add, yet Y is determined by X, so they are dependent.
Distractors assume zero covariance implies independence or that dependence forces a nonzero covariance.

items.prompt: In a game show a car is behind one of three doors. You pick door 1. The host, who does not know where the car is, opens door 3 at random and it happens to show a goat. What is the probability you win by switching to door 2?
rubric: Because the host could have revealed the car, the observation is equally likely under car at 1 or 2, so each has probability 1/2.
2/3 applies the classic problem where the host knowingly avoids the car.

items.prompt: Pick the option with the highest expected payoff among those whose standard deviation is at most 4. A: 20 with probability 0.3 else 0. B: 8 with probability 0.7 else 0. C: 5 for certain. D: 12 with probability 0.4 else 0.

options.label: C: 5 for certain
B: 8 with probability 0.7, else 0
D: 12 with probability 0.4, else 0
A: 20 with probability 0.3, else 0

rubric: B has mean 5.6 and SD about 3.7, so it is feasible and beats C's mean of 5.
A has the top mean of 6 but SD about 9.2; D has mean 4.8 and SD about 5.9.

items.prompt: A call centre's hourly call counts have mean 10 and variance 30 over many weeks. An analyst proposes Poisson(10) with a 99th-percentile rule for staffing. Judge this plan.

options.label: Sound: the Poisson fits any count data, and the larger variance only reflects sampling noise over many weeks
Sound: the Poisson mean matches the data, and matching the mean is all a staffing percentile rule needs
Flawed: counts must be binomial, because hours form a fixed number of trials with a fixed success chance
Flawed: Poisson forces variance to equal the mean, so tails are underestimated; use an overdispersed model

rubric: Variance three times the mean signals overdispersion, so a Poisson percentile would understate peaks.
Distractors treat a matching mean as sufficient or wrongly demand a binomial model.

items.prompt: Devices receive random IDs, uniform and independent, from 2^b values. With 500 devices, which is the smallest b among these that keeps the collision probability below 1%?
rubric: Collision probability is about n(n-1)/(2N); for b = 24 it is about 0.74%, while b = 20 gives about 11%.
16 and 20 underestimate the birthday effect; 32 works but is not the smallest.

items.prompt: A forensic match has a 1-in-1,000,000 chance of occurring for an innocent person. A city has 5,000,000 people and no other evidence points to the suspect. Judge the claim 'there is only a one-in-a-million chance the suspect is innocent'.

options.label: Invalid: the probability should be 5 in 1,000,000, because the city is five times larger than one million people, so the risk scales with population
Valid: with no other evidence, a rare match makes innocence as unlikely as the match is to occur by chance, since the base rate adds nothing
Invalid: it confuses P(match | innocent) with P(innocent | match); about five innocent people would match, so guilt is uncertain
Valid: the match probability for an innocent person equals the probability that this particular suspect is innocent, as both describe the same event

rubric: This is the prosecutor's fallacy: the posterior depends on the base rate, and with about 5 expected random matches the suspect is only one of several.
Distractors transpose the conditional or rescale the figure without Bayesian reasoning.

items.prompt: A safety report needs a guaranteed bound on P(|X - 50| >= 15) for response times X, which are skewed with unknown distribution, mean 50 and SD 5. Which statement is best justified?

options.label: About 0.3%, from the normal 3-SD rule, which is accurate enough for skewed data like response times
Exactly 0, since values beyond 3 SD from the mean cannot occur in any real data set
At most 1/9, by Chebyshev, which needs only the mean and SD and holds for any distribution
At most 1/3, by Markov, since the mean alone bounds how often a value strays 15 from it

rubric: Chebyshev gives 25/225 = 1/9 with no distributional assumption, meeting the guarantee criterion.
The normal rule is not a guarantee for skewed data, and Markov does not bound deviations from the mean.

items.prompt: An analyst must choose defensible probability models. Which choices are defensible? Select all that apply.

options.label: Count of rare independent events in a long fixed interval, modelled as Poisson since events are rare and independent
Defective count in 20 items sampled from a lot of 10,000, modelled as binomial since the sample is a tiny fraction
Defective count in 50 items sampled from a lot of 60, modelled as binomial since each item is defective or not
Waiting time for the next event in a Poisson process, modelled as exponential since the rate is constant
Number of rolls until the first six, modelled as binomial since each roll is a trial with probability 1/6

rubric: Binomial approximates sampling without replacement only when the sample is a small fraction of the population; Poisson and exponential fit rare independent events at a constant rate.
Sampling most of a small lot needs hypergeometric, and the number of trials until first success is geometric, not binomial.

items.prompt: A clinic screens for a condition with 2% prevalence. The test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity, with errors independent across repeat tests. Treatment is risky, so policy requires at least 50% of treated patients to truly have the condition. Which policy meets this requirement?

options.label: Treat after one positive test, since 95% sensitivity means most of those treated truly have the condition
Treat after two positives in two tests, since repeating the test cuts false positives enough to pass 50%
Treat everyone without testing, since that guarantees no affected patient is missed or left untreated
Treat after at least one positive in two tests, since a second chance to detect cases raises the share correct

rubric: Two positives give PPV = 0.02*0.9025 / (0.02*0.9025 + 0.98*0.01), about 65%, which exceeds 50%.
The other policies yield PPV under 50%; 'at least one of two' raises false positives.

items.prompt: A colleague claims: "If P(A|B) > P(A), then P(B|A) > P(B)", for events with positive probabilities. Which evaluation is correct?

options.label: True only if P(A) = P(B), because otherwise the two conditional probabilities scale differently
False in general, because conditional probabilities are not symmetric and P(B|A) can fall even when P(A|B) rises
False unless A and B are mutually exclusive, because overlap breaks the symmetry in Bayes' rule
True, because both inequalities are equivalent to P(A and B) > P(A)P(B) when P(A) and P(B) are positive

rubric: Both conditions reduce to P(A and B) > P(A)P(B), so positive association is symmetric.
Distractors confuse the asymmetry of P(A|B) versus P(B|A) values with asymmetry of the direction of dependence.

items.prompt: An argument says: "If A, B and C are pairwise independent, then P(A and B and C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)." Which critique is correct?

options.label: Flawed only when events overlap; if A, B and C are disjoint with positive probabilities, then the triple product rule always holds for them
Valid for fair events with probability 1/2 each, since the triple product then equals 1/8 by symmetry of the events
Valid: pairwise independence implies the triple product rule, because P(A and B and C) factors through P(A and B) and P(C)
Flawed: with two fair flips, A = first heads, B = second heads, C = flips match, pairs are independent but P(all) = 1/4

rubric: The coin counterexample shows pairwise independence does not give mutual independence.
Distractors assume factorisation extends automatically or confuse disjointness with independence.

items.prompt: A call centre's daily call counts have mean 20 and variance 85. Staffing must cover the 99th percentile of daily calls. An analyst proposes a Poisson model. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Use a Normal with the same mean and a matching variance of 20, since for large counts the Normal approximates Poisson tail quantiles well and the sample variance can be ignored
Switch to a Binomial model, since capping the count at n pushes the variance below the mean and tightens the tails, which gives a more reliable 99th percentile
Keep Poisson, since count data of this kind is always Poisson and the extra variance is just sampling noise that will average out over more days
Use a negative binomial or Poisson mixture, since variance far above the mean signals varying rates that Poisson cannot capture

rubric: Poisson forces variance = mean; overdispersion means 99th percentile would be underestimated.
Distractors ignore overdispersion or choose models that cannot raise variance above the mean.

items.prompt: A game pays 2^k dollars if the first head appears on toss k of a fair coin. The expected payout is infinite. The casino can pay at most 2^20 dollars (payouts capped there). Which judgement about a fair entry price is best?

options.label: Infinite, because the capped game still has unbounded outcomes in principle and the expectation is unchanged
About $1,048,576, because a fair price must equal the largest payout the casino could ever owe a player
About $2, because the median payout is a better price than the mean for heavy-tailed games like this one
About $21, because each toss count up to 20 adds about $1 and the capped tail adds about $1 more

rubric: Each toss count k up to 20 contributes 1 dollar, and the capped tail contributes about 1, giving about 21.
Distractors keep the uncapped infinite expectation or substitute median or maximum for the mean.

items.prompt: A disease has 0.1% prevalence. A test has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity. A clinic says a positive result means the patient is 99% likely to be ill. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: Overstated: about 95%, since specificity bounds how often a positive result is correct for a patient
Overstated: about 2%, since false positives from the healthy 99.9% far outnumber true cases
Roughly right, since a sensitivity of 99% is the chance that a positive result is a true case
Understated: about 50%, since the two error rates roughly balance and so cancel each other out

rubric: Distractors confuse P(positive|ill) with P(ill|positive), the base-rate error.

items.prompt: Evaluate these claims about independence and correlation for random variables with finite variances. Which are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Independent variables are always uncorrelated
If X and Y are jointly normal and uncorrelated, then they are independent
Uncorrelated variables are always independent
If X is uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2, then X and Y are uncorrelated yet dependent
Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) can hold only if X and Y are independent

rubric: Independence implies zero covariance; the X, X^2 example shows the converse fails; joint normality is the special case where it holds.
Var(X+Y) additivity needs only zero covariance, so the last claim and the 'uncorrelated implies independent' claim are false.

items.prompt: On a game show you pick door 1 of 3. The host, who does not know where the car is, opens door 3 at random and it happens to show a goat. A friend says: "Always switch, it wins 2/3 of the time." Which evaluation is correct?

options.label: Right: switching wins 2/3 because the remaining door inherits door 3's 1/3 chance of hiding the car, so it now holds 2/3
Wrong: staying wins 2/3 because the goat reveal adds information in favour of your original pick over the other door
Wrong here: staying and switching each win 1/2, because the reveal was not guaranteed to be a goat
Right: switching wins 2/3 because your first pick had only a 1/3 chance and nothing about that has changed since

rubric: P(car behind 1 | goat revealed at random) = (1/3)/(1/3 + 2/3 * 1/2) = 1/2.
Distractors apply the standard Monty Hall result, which relies on a host who knowingly avoids the car.

items.prompt: You have a coin with unknown bias p (0 < p < 1) and independent flips. Design a procedure that produces an exactly fair bit. Which design works?

options.label: Flip once and report the opposite of the result, since inverting swaps p and 1-p evenly
Flip twice; HT means heads, TH means tails, and on HH or TT repeat the pair of flips
Flip three times and report the majority, since majority voting removes any bias in the coin
Flip twice and report the first flip if the two differ; if they match, report a fresh third flip

rubric: HT and TH both have probability p(1-p), so the accepted outcomes are equally likely.
Distractors yield outcomes with unequal probabilities such as p^2 versus (1-p)^2.

items.prompt: Design a one-pass method that keeps exactly one item chosen uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length, using O(1) memory. Which design meets both constraints?

options.label: Keep the nth item with probability 1/2, replacing the stored one, so recent items are equally likely
Keep the nth item with probability 1/n^2, so the total replacement chance converges to a constant
Keep the first item only and ignore the rest, since random arrival order makes it uniform over the stream
Keep the nth item with probability 1/n, replacing the stored one, so each item ends up equally likely

rubric: Item i survives with probability (1/i)(i/(i+1))...((n-1)/n) = 1/n.
Distractors give geometrically biased or fixed-position selection.

items.prompt: You need a nonnegative random variable X with E[X] = 10 that makes P(X >= 100) as large as Markov's inequality allows. Which distribution does this?
rubric: Mean 10 with all mass at 0 and 100 gives P(X>=100) = 0.1, the Markov bound.
Distractors have the wrong mean (19, 20) or never reach 100.

items.prompt: You will assign random IDs uniformly from N = 2^b values to 10,000 items. Design the ID length: what is the smallest b keeping the probability of any collision below 1% (use the birthday approximation 1 - exp(-n^2/(2N)))?

options.label: 27 bits
30 bits
33 bits
40 bits

rubric: Need N >= about 5.0e9, and 2^32 gives about 1.2% while 2^33 gives about 0.6%.
Smaller values ignore the n^2 growth; 40 bits works but is not the smallest.

items.prompt: You must estimate an event probability near 1e-6 with relative error under 10% using at most 100,000 simulations, so naive sampling expects about 0.1 hits. Which design meets the constraints?

options.label: Sample from a shifted distribution where the event is common, and weight each hit by its likelihood ratio
Sample from a shifted distribution where the event is common and report the raw hit fraction without weights
Run naive Monte Carlo and report the observed hit fraction, since the law of large numbers guarantees accuracy
Run naive Monte Carlo and count zero hits as one hit, since one hit is the smallest estimable frequency

rubric: Importance sampling with likelihood-ratio weights gives an unbiased estimate with enough hits.
Distractors rely on naive sampling or drop the weights that correct the bias.

items.prompt: Using only fair coin flips, you must simulate a fair six-sided die exactly (each face probability 1/6), terminating with probability 1. Which designs meet both constraints? Select all that apply.

options.label: Flip 4 coins to get a number 0-15; if it is 12 or more repeat, otherwise take it mod 6 and add 1
Flip 3 coins to get a number 0-7 and take it mod 6, adding 1
Flip 10 coins to get a number 0-1023 and take it mod 6, adding 1
Flip 1 coin to pick {1,2,3} or {4,5,6}, then flip 2 coins to pick within the half, repeating the 2 flips on 11
Flip 3 coins to get a number 0-7; if it is 6 or 7 repeat, otherwise add 1

rubric: Each valid design maps equally many equally likely outcomes to each face and rejects the rest.
Mod 6 of 8 or 1024 outcomes gives unequal counts per face, so the result is not exactly uniform.

items.prompt: A supplier ships very large lots with a true defect rate of 2%. You design an acceptance plan: inspect n random items and accept the lot only if none is defective. Constraints: a lot with a 2% defect rate must be accepted at most 5% of the time, and the sample should be as small as possible. Treat draws as independent. Which n meets this?
rubric: n = 100 gives about 13% acceptance; 250 works but is not minimal; 50 is the 1/p heuristic.
